# Three objections, and the answers to them


Three routes are encoded to the conclusion that Scripture is the sole
infallible rule. The classical line reads Scripture as "given by inspiration of
God" and able to make the believer "throughly furnished" (2 Timothy 3:16–17),
sufficient and clear, and holds that Scripture teaches the principle itself.
The eliminative line holds that Scripture is infallible and that no other rule
is. Mark 7's
line is taken in its own chapter. Against them stand three objections, and they
come from different directions, so that answering one does not answer another.

**Self-refutation.** If a doctrine binds only when Scripture teaches it, and
Scripture does not teach sola scriptura, the position fails by its own
standard.

**The canon.** If the canon is known through the Church's reception of it, an
authority outside Scripture is needed to identify Scripture. Augustine gives
the classical form: *ego vero Evangelio non crederem, nisi me catholicae
Ecclesiae commoveret auctoritas*. He would not believe the gospel, he says,
unless the authority of the Catholic Church moved him to.

**The regress of interpretive authority.** Cross and Judisch argue that the
individual keeps the final authority to interpret, exercised indirectly by
choosing which body to submit to. So Tradition I, which gives tradition a real
but subordinate authority, is not distinct in principle from Tradition 0: "when
I submit (so long as I agree), the one to whom I submit is me."

These objections tell against the position this argument sets out, and they
are encoded with the same care, because the project's rules require every
rival to be.

## Does Scripture have to teach the principle?

The first version of this argument said that the whole dispute reduces to one
premise, that Scripture teaches sola scriptura
(`solaScripturaIsTaughtByScripture`). That premise does two jobs, and the jobs
come apart. It is not needed to reach the conclusion, because the eliminative
line delivers the sole rule without it (`hinge_not_load_bearing_for_conclusion`).
It is needed within the classical line taken alone.

Against self-refutation it is one of *two* answers. The objection joins two
grounds, so either may be denied. The classical answer denies that Scripture
fails to teach the principle (`classical_answer_blocks_self_refutation`). The
other denies that the rule about what binds governs a claim about where binding
doctrine comes from (`scoping_blocks_self_refutation`). That is the
final-arbiter reading, on which Scripture is not the only arbiter but the last
one. The objection succeeds only against a position that refuses both.

A second route to the conclusion does not help here, and this is where the
argument parts from sola fide. There, a second strand defeated an attack on a
premise. These objections are not attacks on a premise: each delivers the
denial of the conclusion by itself, so another route to the conclusion does
nothing against them. What answers an objection is denying one of *its*
grounds.

## Parity: "your side has the same problem"

Kruger on the canon and Mathison on interpretive authority make the same move.
They concede the circle, and deny that it tells against one side more than the
other. What the move achieves is that the disputed question comes out
*independent* of the reply's grounds: neither it nor its denial follows,
because two readings satisfy those grounds and disagree about it
(`parity_leaves_the_canon_open`, `parity_leaves_the_distinction_open`). The
replies block the objection, and establish nothing.

Blocking an objection and establishing nothing are one fact here, stated once
for each reply, so the two halves cannot drift apart into different questions.
Barrett's parity reply to Geisler gets the same treatment: the defeat Geisler
claims is left open (`parity_leaves_the_defeat_open`). The reply also does more
than fail to clear the charge of circularity. It grants the charge as one of
its own grounds (`circle_parity_concedes_the_charge`).

## The circle inside Protestantism

Geisler, who holds Tradition 0, charges Tradition I with a circle. The creedal
consensus is said to rest on Scripture's clarity, while Scripture's clear sense
is said to be unobtainable without that consensus. With both legs in place,
neither end is settled either way (`circle_leaves_the_consensus_open`,
`circle_leaves_the_perspicuity_open`). A circle of claims can be held all true
or all false with nothing to choose between them. That charge is made from
inside the Reformation, against the position this argument encodes as the
Protestant one. It is conditional like every result here: deny either leg and
the circle is not there.

## A limitation worth stating

The final-arbiter reading turns on a distinction between **doctrine**, which
needs Scripture to settle it, and **practice** neither commanded nor forbidden,
which does not. That is a distinction of scope, and the logic used here cannot
express one: it works with whole claims, and cannot say "for every doctrine".
So the distinction is carried by how the claims are drawn and by this
paragraph, not by the logic. What the encoding shows is what follows given the
distinction, not that the distinction can be drawn.

## The positions, written out


Besides the Protestant position, Tradition I, these are written out: Tradition
0, as Geisler holds it; Trent, as Tradition II; Tradition III, resting on
Vatican I; the Orthodox position, as Florovsky and Ware state it; the three
objections, each as an argument of its own; and the replies to them. The rivals
were written before anything was proved about the position argued for.

## What follows, and what does not


Each result takes one position, objection or reply and asks whether its
conclusion follows from its premises. Where it does, the result says so. Where
it does not, the result names a consistent way of taking the texts on which
every premise holds and the conclusion fails. Where a reply leaves a question
open, the result says that neither the question nor its denial follows.

The results to read first are the two on whether Scripture must teach the
principle, because they split the premise the first version of this argument
said everything turned on (`hinge_not_load_bearing_for_conclusion`,
`classical_answer_blocks_self_refutation`).

##### How the lines are built

Three routes reach the conclusion — the classical line, the eliminative line,
and Mark 7's, which takes two lines, and whose principle a further line draws
from Jesus' sayings and Paul's letters — three positions deny it, and three
objections attack it from different directions. Two more lines read the council
at Jerusalem (Acts 15), one as the Reformers read it and one as Rome does, and
they deliver opposite answers about the authority of councils. Each rests on a
line about the apostles' office: that it ended with them, or that it continues
in their successors. Two more read Moses' seat (Matthew 23:2–3) the same two
ways, and deliver opposite answers about the teaching office.

Every reply below is written with `Line.onGrounds`: the objection's own line,
with the ground the reply refuses put back as what the reply offers instead.

##### Steps reaching the conclusion

<a id="toSoleRule"></a>
**`toSoleRule`**

Sufficiency and perspicuity, with the prooftexts and the claim that
scripture teaches the principle, yield the sole infallible rule.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- \\((\href{claims.html#claim-1}{P_{1}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-2}{P_{2}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-7}{P_{7}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-8}{P_{8}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-10}{P_{10}}) \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-9}{P_{9}}\\) — *would give:* Scripture is the sole infallible rule of faith

</div>

<a id="eliminativeToSoleRule"></a>
**`eliminativeToSoleRule`**

The eliminative route: scripture is infallible, nothing else is, so
scripture is the *sole* infallible rule. It never asserts that scripture
teaches the principle.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- \\((\href{claims.html#claim-6}{P_{6}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-12}{P_{12}}) \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-9}{P_{9}}\\) — *would give:* Scripture is the sole infallible rule of faith

</div>

<a id="mark7ToPrinciple"></a>
**`mark7ToPrinciple`**

**Mark 7's step**: from Jesus' rebuke of the elders' tradition to the
principle it enacts — God's word judges human tradition. Rated `wellSupported`:
no reader was found who grants the text and denies the principle, and Rome
grants it in so many words (*Dei Verbum* 10). Not `consensus`, because the step
generalises from one pericope.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- \\(\href{claims.html#claim-3}{P_{3}} \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-37}{P_{37}}\\) — *would give:* God's word judges human tradition: no commandment of men may be taught as God's word, and a tradition that voids God's command is void

</div>

<a id="jesusAndPaulToPrinciple"></a>
**`jesusAndPaulToPrinciple`**

**The same principle from Jesus' sayings and Paul's letters**, without Mark 7.
Jesus says that "the scripture cannot be broken" (John 10:35) and that not "one
jot or one tittle" shall pass from the law (Matthew 5:18); Paul says that even
he, or an angel, would be accursed for preaching "any other gospel" than the one
he had preached (Galatians 1:8–9), and warns a church against teaching "after
the tradition of men … and not after Christ" (Colossians 2:8, 20–22). Together
they say what Mark 7 says: God's word judges human tradition. Rated
`wellSupported`: Aquinas grants Galatians 1:8 and the principle with it, and
denies only that every addition is "another gospel" (`jesusAndPaulPrincipleInference`).

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- \\((\href{claims.html#claim-40}{P_{40}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-41}{P_{41}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-42}{P_{42}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-43}{P_{43}}) \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-37}{P_{37}}\\) — *would give:* God's word judges human tradition: no commandment of men may be taught as God's word, and a tradition that voids God's command is void

</div>

<a id="acts15ToCouncilUnderScripture"></a>
**`acts15ToCouncilUnderScripture`**

**Acts 15, as the Reformers read it.** Men from Judaea laid the custom of
Moses on the gentiles as a condition of salvation (15:1); Peter answered with
the gospel, salvation "through the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ" (15:10–11),
and James with Scripture, "as it is written" (15:15–17). So the gospel judged
even the oldest tradition, and the council judged by Scripture. And the
apostles' own office ended with them, so a council after them lacks what the
council at Jerusalem had: it binds only as far as it agrees with the word, and
may err. The last premise is carried in by `apostlesOfficeEndedLine`. Rated
`disputed`: Wilhelm grants the texts and holds that general councils define with
the Spirit's authority (`acts15ReformedInference`).

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- \\((\href{claims.html#claim-44}{P_{44}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-45}{P_{45}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-46}{P_{46}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-59}{P_{59}}) \rightarrow \lnot \href{claims.html#claim-50}{P_{50}}\\) — *would deny:* A general council after the apostles binds with the Holy Spirit's authority, as the council at Jerusalem did, and cannot err

</div>

<a id="acts15ToCouncilWithTheSpirit"></a>
**`acts15ToCouncilWithTheSpirit`**

**Acts 15, as Rome reads it.** The council's letter says "it seemed good to
the Holy Ghost, and to us" (15:28), and its decrees were "delivered" to the
churches "for to keep" (16:4). The council was "the apostles and elders" (15:6,
22–23; 16:4), and the apostles' office did not end with them but continues in
those who succeed them. So a general council binds with the Spirit's authority,
and cannot err. The last premise is carried in by `apostolicSuccessionLine`.
Rated `disputed`: the Westminster Confession cites the same texts for the
authority of councils and denies that councils since the apostles cannot err
(`acts15RomanInference`).

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- \\((\href{claims.html#claim-48}{P_{48}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-49}{P_{49}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-60}{P_{60}} \land \lnot \href{claims.html#claim-59}{P_{59}}) \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-50}{P_{50}}\\) — *would give:* A general council after the apostles binds with the Holy Spirit's authority, as the council at Jerusalem did, and cannot err

</div>

<a id="apostlesToTheirOfficeEnded"></a>
**`apostlesToTheirOfficeEnded`**

**The apostles' office, as the Reformers read it.** The apostle chosen in
Judas's place had to be one who had "companied with us all the time" and was "a
witness with us of his resurrection" (Acts 1:21–22); Paul was the last to see
the risen Christ, "last of all he was seen of me also" (1 Corinthians 15:8);
Peter counts Paul's letters with "the other scriptures" (2 Peter 3:15–16); and
Paul writes as "an apostle" beside "Timothy our brother" (2 Corinthians 1:1;
Colossians 1:1). So the apostles' own office ended with them. Rated `disputed`:
*Lumen Gentium* 20 grants the texts and holds that the apostles' office is
permanent in the order of bishops (`apostlesOfficeEndedInference`).

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- \\((\href{claims.html#claim-54}{P_{54}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-55}{P_{55}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-56}{P_{56}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-57}{P_{57}}) \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-59}{P_{59}}\\) — *would give:* The apostles' own office ended with them; those after them succeed to their ministry, not to their office

</div>

<a id="successionToTheOfficeContinuing"></a>
**`successionToTheOfficeContinuing`**

**The apostles' office, as Rome reads it.** "His bishoprick let another take"
(Acts 1:20); "commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others
also" (2 Timothy 2:2); and Clement records that the apostles appointed bishops
and deacons, with instructions that "other approved men should succeed them in
their ministry" (1 Clement 44). So the apostles' office did not end with them.
Rated `disputed`: Calvin grants the texts and holds that the apostolic office
was not "instituted in the Church to be perpetual"
(`apostolicSuccessionInference`).

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- \\((\href{claims.html#claim-61}{P_{61}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-62}{P_{62}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-63}{P_{63}}) \rightarrow \lnot \href{claims.html#claim-59}{P_{59}}\\) — *would deny:* The apostles' own office ended with them; those after them succeed to their ministry, not to their office

</div>

<a id="mosesSeatToTheWordTaught"></a>
**`mosesSeatToTheWordTaught`**

**Moses' seat, as the Reformers read it.** Jesus bids the crowd observe what
the scribes and Pharisees bid, because they sit in Moses' seat (Matthew
23:2–3); in the same discourse he condemns their teaching on oaths as the
teaching of "blind guides" (23:16–22), and in Mark 7 the elders' tradition as
making void the word of God. So the seat binds only so far as Moses is taught
from it: an office in the Church is heard as far as it teaches God's word, and
not for the seat alone. Rated `disputed`: Cornelius a Lapide grants the texts
and holds that the scribes were to be obeyed in all "not contrary to Moses and
the Law" (`mosesSeatReformedInference`).

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- \\((\href{claims.html#claim-51}{P_{51}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-52}{P_{52}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-3}{P_{3}}) \rightarrow \lnot \href{claims.html#claim-53}{P_{53}}\\) — *would deny:* Those who hold the Church's teaching office are to be heeded for the seat they hold, in whatever is not contrary to God's law, even when they live ill

</div>

<a id="mosesSeatToTheOffice"></a>
**`mosesSeatToTheOffice`**

**Moses' seat, as Rome reads it.** Jesus bids the crowd observe what those in
Moses' seat bid, though "they say, and do not" (Matthew 23:2–3). So the seat
carries an authority of teaching that passes to those who succeed to it, and in
the Church those who hold the teaching office are heeded for the seat they
hold, in what is not contrary to God's law, even when they live ill. Rated
`disputed`: Calvin grants the text and holds that the scribes were to be obeyed
"only so far as they adhere to the pure and simple exposition of the Law"
(`mosesSeatRomanInference`).

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- \\(\href{claims.html#claim-51}{P_{51}} \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-53}{P_{53}}\\) — *would give:* Those who hold the Church's teaching office are to be heeded for the seat they hold, in whatever is not contrary to God's law, even when they live ill

</div>

<a id="principleExcludesMensCommandments"></a>
**`principleExcludesMensCommandments`**

What the principle says of a commandment of men: it may not be bound on the
Church as God's word. This is Isaiah 29:13 as Mark 7:7 quotes it.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- \\(\href{claims.html#claim-37}{P_{37}} \rightarrow \lnot \href{claims.html#claim-38}{P_{38}}\\) — *would deny:* A commandment of men may rightly be bound on the Church as God's word

</div>

<a id="principleToSoleRule"></a>
**`principleToSoleRule`**

**From Mark 7's principle to the sole rule.** If God's word judges human
tradition, and no unwritten tradition can now be shown to be apostolic, so that
none binds as God's word, Scripture is the sole infallible rule. Rated
`disputed`: Geiselmann holds that Scripture contains all revealed content and,
as a Catholic after Vatican I, keeps the Magisterium as its infallible
interpreter; Florovsky holds that tradition adds nothing to
Scripture and keeps the mind of the Church as its interpreter. Neither adds a
word to Scripture; both deny it is the *sole* infallible rule.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- \\((\href{claims.html#claim-37}{P_{37}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-39}{P_{39}}) \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-9}{P_{9}}\\) — *would give:* Scripture is the sole infallible rule of faith

</div>

<a id="tradition0ToSoleRule"></a>
**`tradition0ToSoleRule`**

Geisler's route: the historical-grammatical method suffices, so creeds may
inform without binding, and no second infallible rule is needed.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- \\((\href{claims.html#claim-26}{P_{26}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-25}{P_{25}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-6}{P_{6}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-12}{P_{12}}) \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-9}{P_{9}}\\) — *would give:* Scripture is the sole infallible rule of faith

##### The three objections

<a id="selfRefutationStep"></a>
**`selfRefutationStep`**

If a doctrine binds only when scripture teaches it, and scripture does not
teach sola scriptura, then sola scriptura does not bind.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- \\((\href{claims.html#claim-11}{P_{11}} \land \lnot \href{claims.html#claim-10}{P_{10}}) \rightarrow \lnot \href{claims.html#claim-9}{P_{9}}\\) — *would deny:* Scripture is the sole infallible rule of faith

</div>

<a id="canonObjectionStep"></a>
**`canonObjectionStep`**

If the canon is known only through the Church's reception, and identifying
the canon requires an infallible authority, then an infallible authority
outside scripture is needed to identify scripture.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- \\((\href{claims.html#claim-16}{P_{16}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-17}{P_{17}}) \rightarrow \lnot \href{claims.html#claim-9}{P_{9}}\\) — *would deny:* Scripture is the sole infallible rule of faith

</div>

<a id="interpretiveRegressStep"></a>
**`interpretiveRegressStep`**

Cross and Judisch: if the individual retains ultimate interpretive
authority, exercised indirectly by choosing the body to submit to, then
Tradition I's ministerial authority is not a principled difference from
Tradition 0.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- \\((\href{claims.html#claim-19}{P_{19}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-21}{P_{21}}) \rightarrow \lnot \href{claims.html#claim-20}{P_{20}}\\) — *would deny:* Sola scriptura differs in principle from solo scriptura

</div>

##### Geisler's circle

Two legs, each supplying the other's ground. The consensus of the Church is
said to rest on the clarity of scripture, while the clear sense of scripture is
said to require the consensus of the Church.

<a id="consensusRestsOnPerspicuity"></a>
**`consensusRestsOnPerspicuity`**

Leg one: the creedal consensus rests on scripture's clarity.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- \\(\href{claims.html#claim-8}{P_{8}} \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-27}{P_{27}}\\) — *would give:* The creedal consensus is hermeneutically necessary for understanding scripture

</div>

<a id="perspicuityRestsOnConsensus"></a>
**`perspicuityRestsOnConsensus`**

Leg two: scripture's clear sense is not obtainable without that
consensus.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- \\(\href{claims.html#claim-27}{P_{27}} \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-8}{P_{8}}\\) — *would give:* Scripture is clear on what is necessary for salvation

</div>

##### The replies, as substituted grounds

Each reply is the objection's own line with the ground it refuses replaced by
what the reply offers instead. Adding a premise could never block a valid
argument; taking away the ground it needed is what a reply actually does.

##### Geisler's charge as an argument, and the replies to it

The cycle results above are a formal fact: a cycle of implications grounds
neither end. The line below is the *dialectical* fact — Geisler charging
circularity, and what answers the charge. They are different claims, and both
are worth having.

Every reply denies the second leg, that scripture's clear sense is unobtainable
without the consensus. Barrett's is the exception: it concedes the circle and
denies that circularity is a defect peculiar to Tradition I, which is why
`circleDefeatsLine` carries the universality claim as a ground of its own.

<a id="circleStep"></a>
**`circleStep`**

Both legs together make the reasoning circular.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- \\((\href{claims.html#claim-29}{P_{29}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-30}{P_{30}}) \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-31}{P_{31}}\\) — *would give:* Tradition I's reasoning is circular

line of its own (`mark7Line`).

- (2) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-5}{P_{5}}\\) — 2 Thessalonians 2:15 — hold to the traditions taught by word or letter
- (3) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-28}{P_{28}}\\) — Doctrine develops without new revelation: the deposit is closed
- (4) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-19}{P_{19}}\\) — Tradition carries real but fallible — ministerial — authority

##### How the variants are written

Several packages are built to be *refuted*. A reply is shown to block an
objection by writing the objection's line on the reply's grounds and exhibiting
a countermodel.

The parity replies have no packages at all. What they do is that the disputed
proposition comes out *independent* of the reply's grounds — neither entailed
nor refuted by them — and `Independent` takes a premise list and a formula, so
the reply's `Line` is all it needs.

##### The positions

<a id="protestant"></a>
**`protestant`** — Protestant (sola scriptura as final arbiter)

**The Protestant position**: three routes to the conclusion, on the
final-arbiter reading — the classical, the eliminative, and Mark 7's, whose
principle it also draws from Jesus' sayings and Paul's letters. Scripture
is not the only authority but the only infallible one; tradition is ministerial,
and practices neither commanded nor forbidden need no scriptural warrant. It
reads the council at Jerusalem as the Reformers did: a council after the
apostles binds as far as it agrees with Scripture, and may err, because the
apostles' own office ended with them. And it reads
Moses' seat (Matthew 23:2–3) as Calvin did: an office in the Church is heard as
far as it teaches God's word.

<a id="tradition0"></a>
**`tradition0`** — Tradition 0 (creeds informative, not normative)

**Tradition 0**, as Geisler states it: creeds inform without binding, and
the historical-grammatical method does the work an authoritative interpreter
was supposed to do.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-26}{P_{26}}\\) — The historical-grammatical method alone suffices to obtain the meaning of scripture on essential doctrine
- (2) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-25}{P_{25}}\\) — Creeds are informative without being normative
- (3) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-6}{P_{6}}\\) — Scripture is infallible
- (4) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-12}{P_{12}}\\) — No candidate rule of faith other than scripture is infallible
- (5) \\((\href{claims.html#claim-26}{P_{26}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-25}{P_{25}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-6}{P_{6}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-12}{P_{12}}) \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-9}{P_{9}}\\)
- \\(\vdash\\) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-9}{P_{9}}\\) — *at issue:* Scripture is the sole infallible rule of faith

</div>

No premise here rests on scripture alone.

<a id="tridentine"></a>
**`tridentine`** — Trent (Tradition II)

**Tradition II**, the Tridentine two-source position. Its line delivers the
denial, so the package is not the line as it stands: the question asked of
these premises is whether sola scriptura follows, and the answer is that they
entail its negation.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-5}{P_{5}}\\) — 2 Thessalonians 2:15 — hold to the traditions taught by word or letter
- (2) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-13}{P_{13}}\\) — Tradition is a coordinate source of revelation alongside scripture
- (3) \\((\href{claims.html#claim-5}{P_{5}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-13}{P_{13}}) \rightarrow \lnot \href{claims.html#claim-9}{P_{9}}\\) — *would deny:* Scripture is the sole infallible rule of faith
- \\(\vdash\\) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-9}{P_{9}}\\) — *at issue:* Scripture is the sole infallible rule of faith

</div>

Grounded in scripture alone: 2 Thessalonians 2:15 — hold to the traditions taught by word or letter.

<a id="vaticanI"></a>
**`vaticanI`** — Tradition III (the magisterium as the one real source)

**Tradition III**, resting on Vatican I. Kept separate from `tridentine`
because Mathison argues it escapes several objections to the two-source view
while incurring its own. It reads the council at Jerusalem as Rome does: a
general council binds with the Holy Spirit's authority, because the apostles'
office continues in their successors. And it reads Moses' seat
(Matthew 23:2–3) as Cornelius a Lapide did: those who hold the Church's teaching
office are heeded for the seat they hold.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-14}{P_{14}}\\) — The magisterium is an infallible interpreter of scripture
- (2) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-61}{P_{61}}\\) — Acts 1:20 — his bishoprick let another take

- (11) \\((\href{claims.html#claim-48}{P_{48}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-49}{P_{49}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-60}{P_{60}} \land \lnot \href{claims.html#claim-59}{P_{59}}) \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-50}{P_{50}}\\) — *would give:* A general council after the apostles binds with the Holy Spirit's authority, as the council at Jerusalem did, and cannot err

##### The parity replies

No package here. What a parity reply does is stated as `Independent` over the
reply's own line — see `Results` — and independence is a claim about a premise
set and a proposition, not about a package's conclusion, so one statement asks
the reply both questions: whether it blocks the objection and whether it
establishes the conclusion.

Grounded in scripture alone: 1 Corinthians 15:8 — and last of all he was seen of me also, 2 Peter 3:15–16 — Paul's epistles, which the unlearned wrest, as they do also the other scriptures, 2 Corinthians 1:1; Colossians 1:1 — Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ, and Timothy our brother, Acts 15:1 — except ye be circumcised after the manner of Moses, ye cannot be saved, Acts 15:10–11 — a yoke which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear; through the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ we shall be saved, Matthew 23:16–22 — woe unto you, ye blind guides, which say, Whosoever shall swear by the temple, it is nothing, 2 Thessalonians 2:15 — hold to the traditions taught by word or letter.

<a id="classicalStrandWithoutHinge"></a>
**`classicalStrandWithoutHinge`** — Classical (scripture teaches the principle)

The classical line alone, stripped of the hinge.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-1}{P_{1}}\\) — 2 Timothy 3:16 — all scripture is God-breathed and profitable
- (2) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-2}{P_{2}}\\) — 2 Timothy 3:17 — that the man of God may be complete, equipped for every good work
- (3) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-7}{P_{7}}\\) — Scripture is a sufficient rule of faith
- (4) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-8}{P_{8}}\\) — Scripture is clear on what is necessary for salvation
- (5) \\((\href{claims.html#claim-1}{P_{1}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-2}{P_{2}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-7}{P_{7}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-8}{P_{8}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-10}{P_{10}}) \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-9}{P_{9}}\\)
- \\(\vdash\\) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-9}{P_{9}}\\) — *at issue:* Scripture is the sole infallible rule of faith

##### Geisler's circle

<a id="traditionICircle"></a>
**`traditionICircle`** — Tradition I's hermeneutical circle

Both legs of the circle Geisler alleges in Tradition I, asked for the
consensus.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-8}{P_{8}} \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-27}{P_{27}}\\)
- (2) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-27}{P_{27}} \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-8}{P_{8}}\\) — *would give:* Scripture is clear on what is necessary for salvation
- \\(\vdash\\) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-27}{P_{27}}\\) — *at issue:* The creedal consensus is hermeneutically necessary for understanding scripture

No premise here rests on scripture alone.

##### The positions

<a id="protestant_establishes"></a>
**`protestant_establishes`**

Given the Protestant premises, on any of its three routes, the conclusion
follows.

```lean
theorem protestant_establishes : Establishes protestant
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="tradition0_establishes"></a>
**`tradition0_establishes`**

**Tradition 0 establishes it too.** Geisler rejects Mathison's claim that
tradition is hermeneutically necessary; he does not reject sola scriptura. The
position Mathison calls "solo scriptura" and judges unbiblical and unworkable
reaches the same conclusion by a different route, once it is stated by someone
who holds it rather than by its critic.

```lean
theorem tradition0_establishes : Establishes tradition0
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="tridentineReading"></a>
**`tridentineReading`**

The Tridentine reading, written down: tradition is a coordinate source, so
scripture is not the sole rule.

```lean
def tridentineReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.scriptureIsSoleInfallibleRule => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="tridentine_not_establishes"></a>
**`tridentine_not_establishes`**

The two-source premises do not establish sola scriptura — they entail its
negation.

```lean
theorem tridentine_not_establishes : ¬Establishes tridentine
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="magisterialReading"></a>
**`magisterialReading`**

The post-Vatican I reading: the magisterium is the living interpreter, so
scripture is not the sole infallible rule; and the apostles' office did not end
with them, but continues in the bishops.

```lean
def magisterialReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.apostlesOfficeEndedWithThem => False
    | Claim.scriptureIsSoleInfallibleRule => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="vaticanI_not_establishes"></a>
**`vaticanI_not_establishes`**

Tradition III likewise entails the negation — by a different premise from
Tradition II's, which is why the two are separate packages.

```lean
theorem vaticanI_not_establishes : ¬Establishes vaticanI
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="orthodoxReading"></a>
**`orthodoxReading`**

The Orthodox reading: the mind of the Church interprets infallibly, with no
magisterium and no second source of revelation.

```lean
def orthodoxReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.scriptureIsSoleInfallibleRule => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="orthodox_not_establishes"></a>
**`orthodox_not_establishes`**

Orthodoxy also entails the negation, and on its own premise. Its line is
kept apart from Rome's, because grounding the two on magisterial infallibility
would attribute to Orthodoxy a premise it does not hold.

```lean
theorem orthodox_not_establishes : ¬Establishes orthodox
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

##### The three objections, each valid on its own grounds

<a id="selfRefutation_is_valid"></a>
**`selfRefutation_is_valid`**

The self-refutation objection is valid: granted that only scriptural
doctrine binds and that scripture does not teach sola scriptura, the position
fails by its own standard.

```lean
theorem selfRefutation_is_valid : Establishes selfRefutation
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="canonObjection_is_valid"></a>
**`canonObjection_is_valid`**

The canon objection is valid on its own grounds: if the canon is known
through the Church's reception and identifying it requires an infallible
authority, then an authority outside scripture is needed to identify
scripture.

```lean
theorem canonObjection_is_valid : Establishes canonObjection
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="interpretiveRegress_is_valid"></a>
**`interpretiveRegress_is_valid`**

The interpretive-authority regress is valid on its own grounds. It attacks
something the other two do not: not whether the doctrine is scriptural or
whether the canon can be identified, but whether the authority Tradition I
submits to is anything other than the one submitting.

```lean
theorem interpretiveRegress_is_valid : Establishes interpretiveRegress
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

##### The hinge, in its two roles

`solaScripturaIsTaughtByScripture` does two jobs, and they come apart. It is
not load-bearing for reaching the conclusion, because the eliminative line
reaches it without the hinge. It is load-bearing within the classical strand,
and — the result that matters — it is one of only two things that answer the
self-refutation objection.

<a id="hinge_not_load_bearing_for_conclusion"></a>
**`hinge_not_load_bearing_for_conclusion`**

**The hinge is not load-bearing for the conclusion.** Strip it and the
eliminative line still delivers the sole rule, and so does Mark 7's — each on a
premise of its own that the classical line does not need.

```lean
theorem hinge_not_load_bearing_for_conclusion : Establishes
    protestantWithoutHinge
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="hingeDeniedReading"></a>
**`hingeDeniedReading`**

The reading on which scripture does not teach the principle, and the sole
rule does not follow.

```lean
def hingeDeniedReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.solaScripturaIsTaughtByScripture => False
    | Claim.scriptureIsSoleInfallibleRule => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="hinge_is_load_bearing_within_classical_strand"></a>
**`hinge_is_load_bearing_within_classical_strand`**

Within the classical strand taken alone the hinge is still load-bearing:
remove it and that strand yields nothing.

```lean
theorem hinge_is_load_bearing_within_classical_strand : ¬Establishes
    classicalStrandWithoutHinge
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

##### The two answers to self-refutation

The objection's step is a conjunction, so there are two ways to deny it.
Neither answer is redundant with the other: each removes a different ground,
and the objection succeeds only if both are refused.

<a id="scriptureTeachesItReading"></a>
**`scriptureTeachesItReading`**

The reading on which scripture does teach the principle.

```lean
def scriptureTeachesItReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun x => True
```

<a id="classical_answer_blocks_self_refutation"></a>
**`classical_answer_blocks_self_refutation`**

**The classical answer blocks the objection.** Assert that scripture teaches
the principle and the objection no longer delivers its denial.

```lean
theorem classical_answer_blocks_self_refutation : ¬Establishes
    selfRefutationAnswered
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="finalArbiterReading"></a>
**`finalArbiterReading`**

The final-arbiter reading: scripture adjudicates doctrine rather than
sourcing every binding claim, so the bindingness rule does not apply reflexively
to a claim about where doctrine comes from.

```lean
def finalArbiterReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.onlyScripturalDoctrineIsBinding => False
    | Claim.solaScripturaIsTaughtByScripture => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="scoping_blocks_self_refutation"></a>
**`scoping_blocks_self_refutation`**

**And the final-arbiter answer blocks it too, without the hinge.** It
concedes that scripture does not teach the principle in the sense the objection
requires, and denies instead that the bindingness rule governs a claim of this
kind.

So the objection is defeated on either route, and succeeds only against a
position that refuses both. The dispute does not reduce to the hinge alone.

```lean
theorem scoping_blocks_self_refutation : ¬Establishes selfRefutationUnderScope
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

##### The parity replies, and what they are worth

Kruger on the canon and Mathison on interpretive authority make the same move:
concede the circularity, deny that it discriminates between the positions.

Each gets one result. A premise set that entails neither a proposition nor
its negation leaves that proposition *independent* of it, and blocking the
objection and establishing nothing are the two halves of that single fact.
Foundation names the notion for provability; `Testimony.Logic.Independent` is
its semantic counterpart, and `leaves_open` proves it from the two readings the
premises admit. Stated once, the two halves are checked to be about the same
proposition.

<a id="parityEstablishesNothingReading"></a>
**`parityEstablishesNothingReading`**

The reading on which the parity point is granted and the sole rule still
does not follow: the canon came through the Church, the rival's authority is
self-authenticating too, and scripture is not the sole infallible rule.

```lean
def parityEstablishesNothingReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.scriptureIsSoleInfallibleRule => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="krugerParityReading"></a>
**`krugerParityReading`**

Kruger's reading: the canon's reception is conceded, and the demand for an
infallible identifying authority is refused, because the rival's own authority
is self-authenticating too.

```lean
def krugerParityReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.identifyingCanonRequiresInfallibleAuthority => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="parity_leaves_the_canon_open"></a>
**`parity_leaves_the_canon_open`**

**The parity reply leaves the canon question open.** Granted Kruger's
grounds, the sole infallible rule neither follows nor fails: his own reading
has it, and the reading on which the parity point is conceded and the sole rule
still denied has it not. Both satisfy every premise.

That is the whole of what the reply achieves, in one claim. It blocks the canon
objection — the objection's denial is no longer entailed — and it establishes
nothing, because the conclusion is not entailed either. The parity move is
purely defensive, and this is the form that says so without saying it twice.

```lean
theorem parity_leaves_the_canon_open : Independent canonUnderParity.premises
    (p Claim.scriptureIsSoleInfallibleRule)
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="distinctionUnestablishedReading"></a>
**`distinctionUnestablishedReading`**

The reading on which the parity point is granted and the distinction still
does not follow: tradition is ministerial, choosing an authority is private
judgement, and sola scriptura does not differ in principle from solo
scriptura.

```lean
def distinctionUnestablishedReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.traditionIDiffersInPrincipleFromTradition0 => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="mathisonParityReading"></a>
**`mathisonParityReading`**

Mathison's reading: ministerial authority is retained, and the claim that
the individual keeps ultimate interpretive authority is refused, because
choosing Rome is itself an act of private judgement.

```lean
def mathisonParityReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.individualRetainsUltimateInterpretiveAuthority =>
      False
    | x => True
```

<a id="parity_leaves_the_distinction_open"></a>
**`parity_leaves_the_distinction_open`**

**And the same for interpretive authority.** That choosing an authority is
itself private judgement defeats the charge that Tradition I collapses into
Tradition 0; it does not show that Tradition I differs from it in principle.
Both readings satisfy Mathison's grounds, so his grounds settle the question
neither way.

The same shape, twice, against two different objections — which is the point.
It is a property of the move, not of the objection it answers.

```lean
theorem parity_leaves_the_distinction_open : Independent
    regressUnderParity.premises (p
    Claim.traditionIDiffersInPrincipleFromTradition0)
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

##### Geisler's circle

<a id="neitherEndReading"></a>
**`neitherEndReading`**

The reading on which neither the consensus nor the clarity it is said to
rest on obtains.

```lean
def neitherEndReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.creedalConsensusIsHermeneuticallyNecessary => False
    | Claim.scriptureIsPerspicuous => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="bothEndsHoldReading"></a>
**`bothEndsHoldReading`**

The reading on which both ends of the circle obtain: the consensus is
hermeneutically necessary and scripture is clear. A cycle of implications is
satisfied by this as readily as by the reading on which every node is false,
which is what it means for the cycle to settle nothing.

```lean
def bothEndsHoldReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun x => True
```

<a id="circle_leaves_the_consensus_open"></a>
**`circle_leaves_the_consensus_open`**

**Geisler's circularity charge against Tradition I, shown rather than
alleged.** The creedal consensus is said to rest on scripture's clarity, and
scripture's clear sense is said to be unobtainable without that consensus. Put
both legs in place and the consensus is left *independent* of them: it does not
follow, and neither does its denial.

A cycle of implications is satisfied outright by a valuation on which every
node in it is false, and equally by one on which every node is true. Nothing
enters such a loop from outside, so nothing comes out of it — in either
direction. That second direction is what this result gained when it stopped
being a bare `¬ Establishes`: a circle is not merely silent about whether its
nodes hold, it is silent about whether they fail.

Like every result here this is conditional: deny either leg and the circle is
not there. What it settles is that the charge is structural rather than
rhetorical — and it is made from inside Protestantism, against the position
this module encodes as the Protestant one.

```lean
theorem circle_leaves_the_consensus_open : Independent
    traditionICircle.premises (p
    Claim.creedalConsensusIsHermeneuticallyNecessary)
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="circle_leaves_the_perspicuity_open"></a>
**`circle_leaves_the_perspicuity_open`**

**And the other end is no better off.** The same two legs, asked about
perspicuity instead of the consensus, leave it open in the same way and on the
same two readings.

Both results are needed, and they are not two halves of one claim: a circle has
two ends, and each is a separate proposition the premises fail to settle. What
*is* one claim is each result's own two directions, which is why each is an
`Independent` rather than a pair.

```lean
theorem circle_leaves_the_perspicuity_open : Independent
    traditionICircle.premises (p Claim.scriptureIsPerspicuous)
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

##### Geisler's charge, and the three replies

The cycle results above are a formal fact about a cycle of implications. These
are about the charge as an argument: whether it goes through, and what answers
it. Two replies deny its second leg; Barrett's concedes the circle and denies
that circularity is peculiar to this position.

<a id="geislerCircle_is_valid"></a>
**`geislerCircle_is_valid`**

Geisler's charge is valid on its own grounds: grant that the consensus
rests on scripture's clarity and that scripture's clear sense requires the
consensus, and the reasoning is circular.

```lean
theorem geislerCircle_is_valid : Establishes geislerCircle
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="accountabilityReading"></a>
**`accountabilityReading`**

The reading on which the consensus is a product of scripture rather than a
precondition of reading it.

```lean
def accountabilityReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.perspicuityRequiresCreedalConsensus => False
    | Claim.traditionIReasoningIsCircular => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="accountability_blocks_the_circle"></a>
**`accountability_blocks_the_circle`**

**Allen and Swain's reply blocks the charge.** If the creedal consensus is
established by and accountable to scripture, it is what reading scripture
produces rather than what reading scripture presupposes, and the second leg
fails.

What this costs is worth stating: Geisler quotes Mathison saying that it is "to
the Church that we must turn for the true interpretation of the Scripture" and
that without the early rule of faith "hermeneutical chaos and anarchy" reigns.
If that is Tradition I, the reply defends a weaker position than the one
charged.

```lean
theorem accountability_blocks_the_circle : ¬Establishes
    geislerCircleUnderAccountability
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="scripturallyBoundedOfficeReading"></a>
**`scripturallyBoundedOfficeReading`**

The reading on which scripture bounds the interpretive office, and
perspicuity is claimed only for salvation essentials.

```lean
def scripturallyBoundedOfficeReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.perspicuityRequiresCreedalConsensus => False
    | Claim.traditionIReasoningIsCircular => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="scripturalBounding_blocks_the_circle"></a>
**`scripturalBounding_blocks_the_circle`** ⚗

**The scriptural-bounding reply blocks the charge too, and on scriptural
rather than confessional grounds.**

**What is novel here.** No source was found advancing these texts as an answer
to the circularity charge; the passages are cited and the use is assembled in
this library. Acts 20:32 commends the Ephesian elders to "the word of his
grace" rather than to their own office; Titus 1:9 constitutes the office by
holding to "the trustworthy word as taught"; 1 Peter 5:2–3 forbids domineering.
If scripture bounds the interpretive office, the consensus's own warrant is
read off scripture, so it cannot be a precondition of reading scripture — and
Westminster I.7 restricts the perspicuity claim to what is necessary for
salvation, which is not the set of boundaries the creeds fix.

**What would settle whether it is really new.** Mark Thompson's *A Clear and
Present Word* treats the church-as-interpreter objection at length and was not
available here; Vanhoozer's *Biblical Authority after Babel* covers the same
ground. Either may already make this argument, in which case this result should
be recited to them and the tag dropped.

**What it deliberately does not claim.** That scripture *confers* the office.
Conferral invites the recognition/conferral distinction Mathison presses
against Rome over the canon, and boundedness is all the reply needs. It also
does not escape the regress: a critic may say the texts are read this way
because of a tradition. It moves the dispute to far less contested ground; it
does not leave it.

```lean
theorem scripturalBounding_blocks_the_circle : ¬Establishes
    geislerCircleUnderScripturalBounding
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="universalCircularityReading"></a>
**`universalCircularityReading`**

Barrett's own reading: the circle is granted, it is granted to be
universal, and so it does not defeat this position in particular.

```lean
def universalCircularityReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.circularityDefeatsTraditionI => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="universalityDoesNotAcquitReading"></a>
**`universalityDoesNotAcquitReading`**

The sceptic's reading of the same grounds: the circle is granted and its
universality is granted, and the defeat lands anyway. That every ultimate
authority reasons in a circle is read as a charge against all of them rather
than an acquittal of any — including Tradition I.

```lean
def universalityDoesNotAcquitReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun x => True
```

<a id="parity_leaves_the_defeat_open"></a>
**`parity_leaves_the_defeat_open`**

**Barrett's parity reply leaves the defeat open.** Concede the circle; deny
that it is a defect peculiar to this position, since any appeal to an ultimate
authority is circular. On his grounds the defeat does not follow — and neither
does its failure, because the same grounds are satisfied by the reading on
which universal circularity convicts everyone rather than excusing anyone.

The sixth instance of one move. Kruger on the canon, Mathison on interpretive
authority, Athanasius on ὁμοούσιος, Whitaker on unwritten tradition, Geisler
himself on who may interpret the Old Testament, and now Barrett on perspicuity
— against Geisler, who deploys it himself elsewhere.

**This result is not what it was.** It stood as half of a pair whose other half
asked a *different question of the same premises* — whether the reply clears
the charge of circularity, not whether it blocks the defeat — and the pair was
presented as though the two were complements. Naming the shape exposed that:
an independence claim has to say which proposition is left open, and only one
of the two could be named.

```lean
theorem parity_leaves_the_defeat_open : Independent defeatUnderParity.premises
    (p Claim.circularityDefeatsTraditionI)
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="circle_parity_concedes_the_charge"></a>
**`circle_parity_concedes_the_charge`**

**The reply does not merely fail to clear the charge — it grants it.** This
is the second question, kept because it is worth asking and restated because
the answer is stronger than "establishes nothing". Barrett's grounds include
`traditionIReasoningIsCircular` outright: what the parity move denies is that
the circularity is damaging, not that it is there. A position defended only by
this reply is circular and keeping company, and that now follows from the
reply's own premises rather than from the failure of a rival reading.

```lean
theorem circle_parity_concedes_the_charge : Establishes
    circleParityConcedingTheCharge
-- axioms: propext
```

##### Refusing a ground, and denying it

Every reply above is written the same way, as the objection's own line with a
ground replaced. That shape covers two different moves. A reply can **deny** the
ground — entail its negation — or merely **refuse** it, declining to grant it
without asserting the opposite. A denial is an *attack*, and in a dispute an
attack can defeat (`Testimony.Logic.Dispute`). A refusal attacks nothing: it
takes the ground away, which is what `Line.onGrounds` encodes, and the question
it leaves is an entailment question the results above already answer.

Five of the seven replies here refuse. Each refusal is shown by a reading that
grants the reply's grounds and keeps the refused ground true. The other two
deny, and each denial is an entailment.

<a id="kruger_refuses_rather_than_denies"></a>
**`kruger_refuses_rather_than_denies`**

**Kruger refuses the canon objection's ground; he does not deny it.** On
the reading that grants his grounds and still denies the sole rule, identifying
the canon does require an infallible authority.

```lean
theorem kruger_refuses_rather_than_denies : ¬Entails canonUnderParity.premises
    (∼p Claim.identifyingCanonRequiresInfallibleAuthority)
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="mathison_refuses_rather_than_denies"></a>
**`mathison_refuses_rather_than_denies`**

**Mathison refuses the regress's ground.** Granted his grounds, the
individual may still retain ultimate interpretive authority.

```lean
theorem mathison_refuses_rather_than_denies : ¬Entails
    regressUnderParity.premises (∼p
    Claim.individualRetainsUltimateInterpretiveAuthority)
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="final_arbiter_refuses_rather_than_denies"></a>
**`final_arbiter_refuses_rather_than_denies`**

**The final-arbiter answer refuses the self-refutation objection's ground.**
Scoping the bindingness rule to first-order doctrine does not deny that only
scriptural doctrine binds.

```lean
theorem final_arbiter_refuses_rather_than_denies : ¬Entails
    selfRefutationUnderFinalArbiter.premises (∼p
    Claim.onlyScripturalDoctrineIsBinding)
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="accountability_refuses_rather_than_denies"></a>
**`accountability_refuses_rather_than_denies`**

**Allen and Swain refuse the circle's second leg.** A consensus accountable
to scripture does not, by itself, deny that perspicuity requires the
consensus.

```lean
theorem accountability_refuses_rather_than_denies : ¬Entails
    circleUnderAccountability.premises (∼p
    Claim.perspicuityRequiresCreedalConsensus)
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="scriptural_bounding_refuses_rather_than_denies"></a>
**`scriptural_bounding_refuses_rather_than_denies`**

**The scriptural-bounding reply refuses the same leg.**

```lean
theorem scriptural_bounding_refuses_rather_than_denies : ¬Entails
    circleUnderScripturalBounding.premises (∼p
    Claim.perspicuityRequiresCreedalConsensus)
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="classical_answer_denies_the_ground"></a>
**`classical_answer_denies_the_ground`**

**The classical answer denies the self-refutation objection's ground.** It
asserts that scripture teaches the principle, which is the negation of what the
objection assumes.

```lean
theorem classical_answer_denies_the_ground : Entails
    selfRefutationUnderClassicalAnswer.premises (∼notP
    Claim.solaScripturaIsTaughtByScripture)
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="barrett_denies_the_ground"></a>
**`barrett_denies_the_ground`**

**Barrett denies the ground Geisler's charge needs.** He asserts that every
appeal to an ultimate authority is circular, the negation of what the charge
assumes.

```lean
theorem barrett_denies_the_ground : Entails defeatUnderParity.premises (∼notP
    Claim.everyUltimateAuthorityIsCircular)
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

##### Satisfiability

`Entails` quantifies over the valuations satisfying the premises, so a premise
set with no model entails everything — including the negation of what its own
author intended. A package built from contradictory premises would `Establishes`
its conclusion, the proof would close, and every gate would pass.

Only packages carrying a positive `Establishes` result need checking here. A
package with a `¬ Establishes` result is satisfiable already: its countermodel
is a valuation on which every premise holds.

These are not tagged `@[headline]`. They are claims about the health of the
encoding, not about the dispute.

<a id="everythingHoldsReading"></a>
**`everythingHoldsReading`**

The reading on which every claim in this argument holds at once. Not a
position anyone occupies — it is the witness that the packages built only from
positive grounds are coherent.

```lean
def everythingHoldsReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun x => True
```

<a id="protestantReading"></a>
**`protestantReading`**

The Protestant reading: every claim in this argument holds but two, that a
general council after the apostles binds with the Spirit's authority and cannot
err, and that those who hold the Church's teaching office are heeded for the
seat they hold. The Protestant packages read Acts 15 and Moses' seat as the
Reformers did, and deny both.

```lean
def protestantReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.councilBindsWithTheSpiritsAuthority => False
    | Claim.teachingOfficeHeardByItsSeat => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="protestant_is_satisfiable"></a>
**`protestant_is_satisfiable`**

The Protestant package has a model, so `protestant_establishes` is not
vacuous.

```lean
theorem protestant_is_satisfiable : Satisfiable protestant.premises
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="tradition0_is_satisfiable"></a>
**`tradition0_is_satisfiable`**

Tradition 0's package has a model.

```lean
theorem tradition0_is_satisfiable : Satisfiable tradition0.premises
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="protestantWithoutHinge_is_satisfiable"></a>
**`protestantWithoutHinge_is_satisfiable`**

The Protestant package minus the hinge has a model, so
`hinge_not_load_bearing_for_conclusion` is not vacuous either — which matters,
since a load-bearing result that held only because its premises were
contradictory would be precisely backwards.

```lean
theorem protestantWithoutHinge_is_satisfiable : Satisfiable
    protestantWithoutHinge.premises
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="geislerCircle_is_satisfiable"></a>
**`geislerCircle_is_satisfiable`**

Geisler's charge has a model.

```lean
theorem geislerCircle_is_satisfiable : Satisfiable geislerCircle.premises
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="circleParityConcedingTheCharge_is_satisfiable"></a>
**`circleParityConcedingTheCharge_is_satisfiable`**

Barrett's parity grounds have a model — the sceptic's reading, which grants
the circle, grants its universality, and lets the defeat land.

```lean
theorem circleParityConcedingTheCharge_is_satisfiable : Satisfiable
    circleParityConcedingTheCharge.premises
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="selfRefutationOwnReading"></a>
**`selfRefutationOwnReading`**

The world the self-refutation objection describes: scripture does not teach
the principle, so the sole rule does not bind.

```lean
def selfRefutationOwnReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.solaScripturaIsTaughtByScripture => False
    | Claim.scriptureIsSoleInfallibleRule => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="selfRefutation_is_satisfiable"></a>
**`selfRefutation_is_satisfiable`**

The self-refutation objection has a model.

```lean
theorem selfRefutation_is_satisfiable : Satisfiable selfRefutation.premises
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="canonObjectionOwnReading"></a>
**`canonObjectionOwnReading`**

The world the canon objection describes: the canon comes through the
Church, so scripture is not the sole infallible rule.

```lean
def canonObjectionOwnReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.scriptureIsSoleInfallibleRule => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="canonObjection_is_satisfiable"></a>
**`canonObjection_is_satisfiable`**

The canon objection has a model.

```lean
theorem canonObjection_is_satisfiable : Satisfiable canonObjection.premises
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="interpretiveRegressOwnReading"></a>
**`interpretiveRegressOwnReading`**

The world the regress describes: sola scriptura does not differ in
principle from solo scriptura.

```lean
def interpretiveRegressOwnReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.traditionIDiffersInPrincipleFromTradition0 => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="interpretiveRegress_is_satisfiable"></a>
**`interpretiveRegress_is_satisfiable`**

The interpretive-authority regress has a model.

```lean
theorem interpretiveRegress_is_satisfiable : Satisfiable
    interpretiveRegress.premises
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```
